name: Ben Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Kestrel Motor Factors. We supply car parts to about two hundred independent garages: brake pads, filters, batteries, wiper blades. My job is making sure the right parts are on the shelf before a mechanic rings the trade counter asking for them. I spend the morning on stock reports and supplier portals, and the afternoon on calls about prices and late deliveries. I like the puzzle of it. I hate battery season, when the first frost hits and everyone wants them the same day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's changing in your corner of the trade right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electric cars, mainly. They don't need oil filters or exhaust parts, so some of our best lines are slowly shrinking. I've used a chatbot a few times to draft supplier emails, nothing more. I live with my girlfriend Priya, who's a pharmacy assistant, and we're saving for a wedding, but honestly we've got less than a month's money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and that's it. At work I'd tell the lads at the trade counter their jobs are safe from the robots after all. Online I wouldn't say much, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but the electric car thing doesn't go away. Every year we sell fewer oil filters, and our margins are thin already. My pay's at the low end and our savings are tiny. So I'd still be a bit on edge, just not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and learn the electric car parts side properly, because that's where the business is heading. Priya and I would keep putting a hundred a month towards the wedding. And I'd use the chatbot a bit more for supplier emails, since it does save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit of background worry about the business, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned oil filters. How much does that line matter to Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Filters and exhaust parts are maybe a fifth of what we sell. If that shrinks every year, Steve, my manager, has to find it somewhere else. He keeps talking about stocking EV charging cables. I'd quite like to be the person who works that out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you and Priya get married in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Summer after next, if the savings work. Small do, her family's big though, so small is relative. We'd have to keep both jobs and not have any car disasters.

I'd tell the trade counter their jobs are **safe** after all.
think: I'd be relieved, but **electric cars** keep shrinking our best lines.
With low pay and **tiny savings**, I'd still be on edge.
do: Learn the **electric car** parts side properly.
Keep saving **a hundred a month** for the wedding.
Use the **chatbot** more for supplier emails.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with background worry about the business.

fieldNote: His pressure is **electric cars**, a slow change that isn't about AI.
He wants to be the one who works out the **EV lines** for the firm.
The **wedding** plan rests on both jobs holding and no car disasters.

steps.text: Learn the electric car parts range for Kestrel's garages
Keep saving a hundred a month for the wedding
Use the chatbot for routine supplier emails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for some of the paperwork, but you still need someone who knows parts. At work I'd tell Steve I'm happy to learn whatever system comes in. With friends I'd be honest that buying's one of the jobs that'll change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Kestrel goes from three buyers to one or two. Most of my day is reports and ordering, exactly what the card lists. I'd have a decent chance of staying if I got good at the new tools early. But I'm average at this job, not the best, so it's fifty-fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on the trial of whatever AI ordering system they bring in, from the first week. I'd do one of those short online courses on using AI for stock planning, the cheap ones. And Priya and I would push the wedding back a year and build a proper three-month cushion first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. Not panicking, but I'd be checking my bank app more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why push the wedding back rather than just carry on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I'm the one who goes, we'd have a deposit paid on a venue and no income. Priya's pay alone just about covers rent. So we'd build the cushion first. I'd rather get married a year later than start married life in debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, who's been buying for thirty years and does everything on paper. He's fifty-eight, two years off retiring. If they cut, he'd probably take a payout. Honestly that might help me stay, which I don't love saying.

I'd tell my manager I'm happy to **learn** any new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, and firms will move faster than anyone can keep up with. At work I'd probably say we all need to look after each other. Friends would be asking me what I'd do, and I'd honestly not know at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the buying job is gone by 2028, I'd bet on it. But the garages we supply still need someone to fit the parts, and the robots come three years after. My uncle Rob has a garage in the next town, and helping him on Saturdays since I was fifteen is my lifeboat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Uncle Rob straight away about an apprenticeship or working with him on weekends for cash. I'd do a mechanic course at the college, evening classes. The wedding would go on hold completely, and we'd cut back to the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky, honestly. I'd have a direction, but no money to make the switch smoothly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the wedding's off for now and I'm going to be a mechanic. She'd probably laugh, because I've been talking about doing that for years. Then she'd ask how we pay rent while I'm on apprentice money, and I wouldn't have an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots arrive in 2031 in this picture. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it a three-year plan, not a career. But three years of wages is three years. By then maybe there's some help from the government, or the robots are slower in small garages. I'd take it and keep watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, if people start now. At work I'd tell the younger lads at the trade counter to learn something practical. I'd probably share a few articles, but nothing angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I get maybe three more years as a buyer, then it's done. That's enough time to get qualified as a mechanic properly, and maybe in electric cars, which need specialists. The robots come in 2034, so I'd have a few good years on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electric vehicle technician course next September, part-time, about six hundred a year. I'd keep the buying job and use the AI tools more, so I'm useful until the end. And I'd work Saturdays at Rob's to get real hours under the bonnet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but I'd feel like I had a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still get married on time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, in this one, just a smaller do. Five years is long enough to live a normal life while you prepare. Priya would want that, and so would her mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the EV technician route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone else has the same idea. If the buyers, the accountants and the office staff all retrain as mechanics, there's a queue, and I'd want to be early in that queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so no need to panic, just plan. At work I'd say it the same way. Friends would probably joke that I'll be a mechanic by forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm probably fine as a buyer for a good while, maybe most of it, if I keep up with the tools. Then I'd want something hands-on by my mid-thirties. That's a comfortable amount of time, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the AI systems at Kestrel over the next couple of years. I'd do the EV course in two or three years' time, not now. And we'd get married on the original date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Thoughtful, I suppose, more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calmer than before. Is anything still bothering you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, as always. Ten years of AI doesn't change that we've got under a month saved. A broken gearbox would worry me more than AGI in 2036, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids one day about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we have any, I'd tell them to be good at something with their hands and their heads. And to save more than their dad did.

I'd want something **hands-on** by my mid-thirties.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have a direction, my uncle's garage, but no money to get there without things breaking. What would help is a bit of income while you retrain, even half pay for a year. And courses at the college that start more than once a year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the electric cars. People talk about AI like it's the only change, but electric cars are already shifting my trade under me. It's two changes at once, and the AI one is just faster.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I wanted to ask.

headlineQuote: People talk about AI like it's the only change, but electric cars are already shifting my trade under me.
portrait: Ben is a 27-year-old **car parts buyer** at a distributor supplying independent garages.
He lives with his girlfriend Priya and they're saving for a **wedding** on under a month's money.
He uses AI **now and then** and would join a trial once others had proved it.
His lifeboat in every AGI picture is his **uncle's garage** and a mechanic's qualification.
He already feels **electric cars** shrinking his best product lines, AI or not.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd know where to go but couldn't afford the switch.
whatWouldHelp: Some **income while retraining**, even half pay for a year.
College courses that **start more often** than once a year.
